title: SYSK Selects: How Pinball Works
summary: SYSK Selects rerun of the episode on how pinball works, chosen by Josh Clark and recorded in September 2014. The hosts trace pinball's history from 19th-century bagatel tables and Montague Redgrave's spring-loaded ball shooter, through the 1930s explosion of features (coin operation, tilt, bumpers, back glass), the introduction of flippers with Gottlieb's Humpty Dumpty and Genco's Spot Bowler, and the 1940s and 1950s bans led by Mayor LaGuardia in New York. They cover Roger Sharp's 1970s city council demonstration that helped legalize pinball, the decline with video games, Bally/Williams' Pinball 2000, Stern's dominance and new competitors, and collecting. The episode then explains the mechanics: playfield, flippers, ball, black box and back glass, electro-mechanical and solid-state components, solenoid plungers, scoring and multiball, replays and match, and the tilt mechanism and slam tilt. A listener mail segment about parasitic infection concerns closes the episode.

segments.title: Selects intro and Vegas banter
segments.summary: Josh introduces this SYSK Selects pick, How Pinball Works, recorded September 2014. The hosts open with banter about Las Vegas and pinball machines.

segments.title: Early history: bagatel table and the spring shooter
segments.summary: Pinball's lineage goes back to 19th-century bagatel tables. In the 1830s Montague Redgrave added a spring-loaded ball shooter. Players paid the ball keeper for balls and could win prizes.

segments.title: 1930s innovation, Depression popularity, and Chicago
segments.summary: In the 1930s many pinball features appeared, including coin operation, the back glass, electricity, tilt, bumpers and scorekeeping. Cheap entertainment during the Great Depression boosted popularity. The industry was crowded, then consolidated, and Chicago became the pinball capital.

segments.title: Flippers and the shift to a game of skill
segments.summary: Before flippers, players could only nudge the machine, so pinball was closer to chance. Flippers made it a game of skill. Gottlieb's Humpty Dumpty is cited as the first modern game, and Spot Bowler in the 1950s had the first modern flipper arrangement.

segments.title: Pinball bans and LaGuardia's raids
segments.summary: Pinball was outlawed in many US cities, including New York, after being equated with gambling. Mayor LaGuardia ordered raids and the machines were smashed and dumped in the river, including after Pearl Harbor. From the 1940s to the mid 1970s, play was often limited to back rooms of shops.

segments.title: Roger Sharp saves pinball at City Council
segments.summary: At a New York City Council hearing, Roger Sharp demonstrated that pinball was a game of skill. He used a Babe Ruth-style call to aim a shot up the middle, and the council reportedly then repealed the ban. The hosts discuss his later ranking and his son Zach Sharp and son Josh Sharp as top players.

segments.title: Decline, Pinball 2000, and the modern revival
segments.summary: Video games caused pinball's decline, and by the 1990s few manufacturers remained. Bally and Williams produced Pinball 2000, a hybrid with video elements that was not successful. Stern became the main maker, then Jersey Jack formed and competition returned. Home buyers now make up a large share of sales, and vintage machines are re-imported from overseas.

segments.title: How a pinball game is built: ball, playfield, flippers
segments.summary: A pinball game has a ball and flippers, with the aim of scoring points off bumpers and targets while keeping the ball from the drain. The steel ball is about 1 1/16 inches in diameter, weighs about 2.8 ounces and can reach about 90 mph. The playfield is tilted about six to seven degrees and is made of wood.

segments.title: Black box, back glass, and electro-mechanical vs solid state
segments.summary: The black box connects the playfield to the back glass and holds the electronics. Solid-state electronics arrived in the 1970s for scoring, while the playfield mechanisms stayed electro-mechanical. A game has about half a mile of wiring. Solenoids now launch the ball automatically.

segments.title: Scoring, multiball, replays and match
segments.summary: Scoring is driven by combination shots and game-within-a-game modes such as High Roller's poker and casino sequence leading to a Wizard Award and multiball. Replay awards come at score thresholds, and the match feature gives a random chance at a free game based on the last two digits of the score.

segments.title: Tilt mechanism and slam tilt
segments.summary: The tilt mechanism prevents players from cheating by moving the machine. A pendulum-like metal ballast inside a copper ring completes a circuit when tilted too far, giving warnings and then disabling flippers and costing a ball. A slam tilt, detected by leaf switches, shuts the game down.

segments.title: Further resources and closing chat
segments.summary: The hosts recommend the documentaries Special Winlet and Tilt, a Popular Mechanics article, and the HowStuffWorks pinball article. They also discuss the Netflix queue.

segments.title: Listener mail: parasitic infection and patient concerns
segments.summary: Via Tyler Murphy, a listener shares a doctor's account of patients who bring in lint, hair and debris, believing it is parasites. The doctor explains why antiparasitic medication is not used without evidence and says the patient's symptoms still need treatment.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts thank listeners and point to social media, email, and the website for feedback.
